newsitem.title: USA: Most IMM currency futures weak, but pounds jump.
newsitem.headline: Most IMM currency futures weak, but pounds jump.

text.p: IMM currency futures opened mostly lower and extended declines in quiet early dealings, with marks continuing their slump but British pounds soaring to a new six-month high.

Traders and analysts said the focus in currency markets was returning to the economic fundamentals, with a rising interest rate environment supporting sterling while expectations for a soft single European currency continued to undermine the mark.
The Bank of England Thursday raised interest rates 25 basis points to 6.75 percent, the third hike in three months.
The market is devaluing the mark in anticipation of a weak Euro, but Britain is not a participant in European Monetary Union, noted one currency analyst.
And while the more-liquid Swiss franc is attractive as a flight-to-quality currency, widening interest rate differentials favor the pound, he said.
"If you want to buy Europe, England is the place to be," the analyst said.
September pound futures notched a high of $1.6960 in early trading, surpassing the previous six-month high of $1.6910 reached Tuesday in anticipation of the UK rate increase.
The rally places September pounds within striking distance of the $1.7024 contract high registered Jan. 2 and Dec. 31.
Swiss franc futures retreated in early action after hitting a two-week peak of $0.6968 on Thursday.
Mark futures forged yet another contract low at $0.5670 in pit trade, continuing a two-week trend of lower lows registered almost daily.

The currency analyst said Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's remarks Thursday regarding the importance of a strong mark entering EMU could be viewed as counterproductive unless backed up with concrete action to bolster the currency.

This morning, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the country's total public sector deficit in 1997 would be 110 billion marks, or 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, in line with Maastricht Treaty requirements for countries entering EMU.
IMM traders said this morning's release of June U.S. producer price index data sparked little interest in currency futures. "PPI did nothing in the market," one trader said.
Producer prices fell 0.1 percent in June from May, the six consecutive monthly drop. Core producer prices excluding food and energy rose 0.1 percent, in line with expectations.
Yen futures edged lower in what some saw as a low-volume countertrend move but were largely overshadowed by activity elsewhere.
"The yen has been upstaged by the action in the European currencies," the analyst said.

September yen futures were down $0.000051 at $0.008871, marks down $0.0056 at $0.5678, Swiss francs down $0.0046 at $0.6905, sterling up $0.0066 at $1.6914, Canadian dollars up $0.0015 at $0.7327, Australian dollars up $0.0011 at $0.7440 and Mexican pesos up $0.000425 at $0.124475.
